what_its_for: Risankizumab-rzaa is used to treat moderate to severe plaque psoriasis (a skin condition that causes red, scaly patches), psoriatic arthritis (joint pain and swelling related to psoriasis), Crohn's disease (long-term inflammation of the digestive tract), and ulcerative colitis (inflammation and sores in the large intestine). It works by blocking a specific protein in your immune system called IL-23 that causes inflammation.
how_to_take: This medicine is given as an injection under the skin (subcutaneous) or into a vein (intravenous infusion), depending on the condition being treated. For skin and joint conditions, it is usually given as a self-injection under the skin of your stomach, thigh, or upper arm using a prefilled pen or syringe. Your doctor or nurse will teach you how to inject it yourself at home. For Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis, your first doses are given by a healthcare provider as an IV infusion in a clinic, followed by injections under the skin. Always rotate injection sites and never inject into skin that is bruised, red, tender, or hard.
dosing: The dose and schedule depend on the condition being treated. For plaque psoriasis: 150 mg (two 75 mg injections) given once at week 0, week 4, and then every 12 weeks (about every 3 months) after that. For psoriatic arthritis: 150 mg (one or two injections) every 12 weeks. For Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis: three IV infusions are given first (at weeks 0, 4, and 8) in a medical setting, followed by 360 mg injected under the skin every 8 weeks. Your doctor will determine the exact schedule that is right for you.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. Then go back to your regular dosing schedule based on that new date. Do not double up on doses to make up for one you missed. If you are not sure what to do, call your doctor or pharmacist for guidance.
storage: Store the prefilled pens or syringes in the refrigerator at 36°F to 46°F (2°C to 8°C). Keep them in their original carton to protect them from light. Do not freeze and do not shake. If needed, you may store at room temperature (up to 77°F or 25°C) for up to 4 months in the original carton, but do not put it back in the refrigerator after that. Throw away any medicine stored at room temperature that is not used within 4 months. Keep out of reach of children.
what_to_avoid: Do not receive any live vaccines (such as MMR, chickenpox, or nasal flu vaccine) while using this medicine without talking to your doctor first. Avoid close contact with people who have active infections. Tell your doctor before starting this medicine if you have tuberculosis (TB), any chronic infection, or if you have recently been near someone with TB. Do not start this medicine if you have any active infection until it is treated and cleared.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away if you notice any signs of a serious infection such as fever, chills, sweating, cough, shortness of breath, painful urination, or open sores on your skin. Also contact your doctor if you experience any signs of an allergic reaction such as rash, hives, itching, swelling of the face, lips, or throat, or difficulty breathing. Tell your doctor if you develop any new or worsening symptoms, including joint pain, rash, or hair loss (which can sometimes be signs of a rare immune reaction). Always tell all of your healthcare providers that you are taking this medicine before any procedures or vaccinations.
when_it_works: Many patients begin to see improvement in their skin or symptoms within a few weeks, but it may take 3 to 6 months to see the full benefit of this medicine. It is important to keep taking it as prescribed even if you do not notice changes right away. Do not stop taking it without talking to your doctor first.
special_populations: Older adults (65 and over): This medicine can be used in older adults, but they may be at higher risk for infections. Pregnancy: It is not known if this medicine is safe during pregnancy. Talk to your doctor if you are pregnant, plan to become pregnant, or become pregnant while using this medicine. Breastfeeding: It is not known if this medicine passes into breast milk. Discuss the risks and benefits with your doctor before breastfeeding. Children: Safety and effectiveness in children have not been established. Liver or kidney disease: No dose adjustments are typically needed, but always inform your doctor of any health conditions you have.
